seo.title: Whistler ski resort guide
seo.description: North America's largest ski resort: 8,171 acres over two mountains, 1,609 metres of vertical and an 11 km run from the peak to Creekside.
seo.twitterDescription: 8,171 acres, two mountains, 37 lifts and an 11 km run to Creekside.
seo.webpageDescription: Ski facts, terrain by grade per mountain, where to stay and how to get to Whistler in British Columbia.

heroText: Whistler is two mountains on one lift pass, linked at the top by the PEAK 2 PEAK Gondola. Together they hold 8,171 acres and over 200 trails, the vertical runs to 1,609 metres on Blackcomb, and Peak to Creek drops 11 kilometres from the top of Whistler Mountain to Creekside. The summit has averaged 10.4 metres of snow a year over the last ten seasons.

stayOverview: Where you sleep in Whistler decides which gondola you walk to. Whistler Village has both mountain gondolas and the PEAK 2 PEAK; the Upper Village sits at Blackcomb's foot; Creekside is the original 1966 base with its own gondola and easier parking; and Function Junction is the cheap end of the valley, on the highway south.
hotelIntro: Book against high season rather than today's date. Both mountains run on one pass, so the choice between the Village and Creekside is about walking distance and parking, not about which mountain you can ski.
rentalCars: Whistler Village is walkable and both gondolas leave from it, so a car earns its keep mainly for the drive up from Vancouver and for staying at Creekside or Function Junction. The nearest airport is Vancouver, 104 km away.

travelTips.title: One pass, two mountains
travelTips.text: The PEAK 2 PEAK Gondola crosses between Whistler and Blackcomb at altitude, so you can change mountain without skiing down.

travelTips.text: Blackcomb is graded 30% advanced against Whistler's 25%, and both are 55% intermediate.

history.label: 1800s
history.text: Spó7ez was re-populated until it was destroyed by another rock slide in the 1800s.

history.label: 19th century
history.text: In the late 19th century, the Lillooet Cattle Trail was cut through the valley, linking Lillooet via Pemberton with Burrard Inlet via a pass from Squamish to the Seymour River.
The trail was completed in 1877, but because of the difficult and unforgiving terrain, it was only used once for its intended purpose, which was to drive cattle.

history.label: 20th century
history.text: The area began to attract trappers and prospectors—such as John Millar and Henry Horstman—who established small camps in the area in the early 20th century.
The Philips had relocated from Maine to Vancouver in 1910 and had heard rumours of the natural beauty of the area from Pemberton pioneer John Millar.

Completion of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway in 1914 greatly reduced the travel time from three days, providing ease of access from Vancouver, and the Rainbow Lodge gained a reputation as the most popular.
